prompt: An Express route calls `fs.readFileSync` on a 50 MB file for every request. What happens when 100 requests arrive at once?

options: Requests are served one after another, and every other request on the server (even health checks) waits while each read runs

mcq.explanation: `readFileSync` blocks the single JavaScript thread. Nothing else runs until it returns. `fs.promises.readFile` (or a stream) hands the work to libuv so the event loop stays free.

prompt: One endpoint builds a large report with a 2-second synchronous loop, and p99 latency for every other endpoint jumps while it runs. What is the right fix?

options: Move the computation to a worker thread (or a job queue) so the main thread keeps serving requests
Wrap the loop in `async` / `await` so it runs in the background
Increase `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` to 64
Run more instances of the same handler with `Promise.all`
mcq.explanation: `async` does not make CPU work run elsewhere, and the libuv pool only runs Node's own I/O and crypto jobs. CPU-bound JavaScript needs another thread (`worker_threads`) or another process.

prompt: On Node 20, a promise rejects and no code ever attaches a `.catch` or `try/catch` to it. What happens by default?

The rejection is retried on the next tick
mcq.explanation: Since Node 15 the default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` turns an unhandled rejection into an uncaught exception, which crashes the process. Handle errors where the promise is awaited.

prompt: Eight concurrent `crypto.pbkdf2` calls (async), each taking about 100 ms alone, all finish after roughly 200 ms on an 8-core machine. Why?

options: libuv's thread pool has 4 threads by default, so the jobs run in two waves of four
pbkdf2 always runs on the main thread
Node only uses half of the available cores
The calls are serialised because they share a salt
mcq.explanation: Async crypto, `fs`, `dns.lookup` and zlib share the libuv pool (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`, default 4). Raising it, before the pool is first used, lets more of that work run in parallel.

prompt: Heap usage of a Node API grows steadily until the pod is OOM-killed. A heap snapshot shows a module-level `Map` keyed by request id holding response objects. What is the right fix?

options: Bound the cache (LRU with a max size and TTL), or delete entries when the request finishes
Raise `--max-old-space-size` so the process has more memory
Call `global.gc()` after every request
Switch the `Map` to a plain object
mcq.explanation: Anything reachable from a module-level variable lives for the life of the process. More heap only delays the crash and forced GC cannot free reachable objects; the cache needs an eviction rule.
